blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Performance Management System (PMS) is an overarching framework linking individual performance directly to organizational goals.
Performance Appraisal Methods are divided into Traditional Methods and Modern Methods.
Traditional appraisal methods focus primarily on past accomplishment and personality trait evaluations.
Modern appraisal methods emphasize future potential, objective accomplishment, and multi-source feedback.
Identifying and eliminating Rating Errors is crucial for maintaining objectivity and reliability in appraisals.

blocks.content: Performance Management System (PMS) is a continuous process of identifying, measuring, and developing the performance of individuals and aligning their performance with the strategic goals of the organisation. It goes beyond annual appraisal to include goal-setting, coaching, feedback, and development throughout the year.

cells: PMS Component
Description
Goal Setting / KRA-KPI
Define Key Result Areas (KRAs) and Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) at start of year; SMART goals; cascaded from organisational objectives
Mid-Year Review
Formal check-in at mid-year; progress review; course correction; coaching and feedback
Annual Appraisal
End-of-year formal assessment; rating against KPIs; competency assessment; bell curve distribution in many banks
Development Plan (IDP)
Individual Development Plan :identify training needs; career aspirations; skills to develop
Normalisation / Moderation
Calibration of ratings across departments; reduce bias; ensure fair distribution across the organisation
Reward Linkage
Performance ratings linked to increments, bonus, promotion; performance-linked incentive (PLI) in banks

rows: Graphic Rating Scale, Ranking, Paired Comparison

cells: Method
Description
Merits
Limitations
Ranking Method
Rank employees from best to worst; simple comparison
Simple; inexpensive; identifies best and worst performers clearly
Does not show degree of difference; difficult in large groups; no absolute standards
Paired Comparison
Compare each employee with every other employee; count favourable comparisons
More reliable than simple ranking; systematic
Becomes cumbersome with many employees; n(n-1)/2 comparisons needed
Forced Distribution (Bell Curve)
Assign predetermined percentages to rating categories (e.g., 20% top, 70% average, 10% bottom)
Prevents clustering at top/middle; forces differentiation
Leads to de-motivation; unfair when all employees perform well; peer conflicts
Graphic Rating Scale
Rate employee on various traits/dimensions on scale (e.g., 1–5 or 1–10)
Simple; uniform; quantifiable; easy to understand
Halo effect; subjectivity in trait definitions; rater bias
Checklist Method
Rater checks applicable statements from a list of positive/negative statements
Simple; reduces rater bias; consistent
Rater may not understand all items; weightage not always clear
Essay Method
Free-form written description of employee performance by rater
Flexible; can capture nuance; no constraint of fixed categories
Time-consuming; depends on rater's writing skills; difficult to compare across raters
Critical Incident Method
Record specific critical (exceptionally good or bad) incidents during evaluation period
Behaviour-based; specific feedback; reduces recency bias
Time-consuming recordkeeping; negative incidents may discourage employees
Field Review Method
HR officer interviews managers and records assessment; independent review
More objective; HR adds perspective; reduces leniency bias
Time-consuming; HR may not know employee directly

items: Categorization of methods is frequently tested: Traditional (Graphic Rating Scale, Paired Comparison) vs. Modern (MBO, BARS, 360-Degree Feedback).
Expect direct questions on identifying Rating Errors like Halo Effect, Leniency/Strictness Bias, Central Tendency, and Recency Bias.
Note the distinction between Performance Appraisal (periodic evaluation) and Performance Management (continuous process).

cells: Method
Description
Key Features
MBO (Management by Objectives)
Peter Drucker's concept; manager and employee jointly set SMART objectives at start of period; performance measured against these specific objectives
Participative; objective-based; clear accountability; used extensively in banking sector
360-Degree Feedback
Feedback from multiple sources: self, peers, subordinates, supervisor, customers; holistic view
Multi-rater; reduces bias; development-focused; provides comprehensive view; used by HDFC, SBI for senior managers
Behaviourally Anchored Rating Scale (BARS)
Rate on specific behavioural descriptions for each performance level; anchored to actual job behaviours
Highly accurate; behaviour-specific; reduces subjectivity; requires significant development effort
Behavioural Observation Scale (BOS)
Observe and rate frequency of specific job behaviours; observer rates how often employee demonstrates each behaviour
Frequency-based; objective; directly tied to observable job behaviour
Assessment Centre
Multiple simulation exercises (in-basket, role play, group discussion, presentation); multiple trained assessors; used for selection AND appraisal
High validity and reliability; predicts management potential; expensive; used in banks for promotion
Balanced Scorecard (BSC)
Kaplan and Norton; four perspectives: Financial, Customer, Internal Process, Learning & Growth; HR BSC aligns HR metrics with business strategy
Strategic alignment; balanced view; used in bank branch performance and HR department performance
Human Resource Accounting (HRA)
Assign monetary value to human assets; measure ROI on HR investments; Flamholtz model; Lev & Schwartz model
HR as investment, not cost; emerging; not yet standardised accounting practice
Error / Bias
Description
Solution
Halo Effect
One outstanding positive trait influences overall rating favourably
Train raters; use BARS; separate competency ratings
Horn Effect
One negative trait unfairly colours overall assessment negatively
Structured appraisal forms; multiple raters
Central Tendency
Rater avoids extremes; rates everyone as average; all ratings cluster in middle
Forced distribution; training to use full scale
Leniency / Strictness Bias
Consistently high (lenient) or consistently low (strict) ratings by same rater
Calibration sessions; normalisation; anchor definitions
Recency Effect
Events near appraisal period dominate; earlier performance forgotten
Critical incident log throughout year; quarterly reviews
Primacy Effect
First impression dominates overall assessment; recent performance discounted
Structured evaluation of all periods; mid-year reviews
Similarity Bias
Rater rates similar employees more favourably ('like me' effect)
Training on bias; diverse rating panels; structured criteria
Attribution Error
Success attributed to luck externally; failure attributed to personal failings of employee
Objective goal-based assessment; separate outcome from effort
Contrast Effect
Rating influenced by previous candidate (in selection) or comparison with other employees rather than absolute standard
Absolute standards; one-at-a-time evaluation against criteria
